mainTopic: How many people must hear a מחאה, how often it must be repeated, and when repeated protests count
overview: The גמרא asks why one opinion says a מחאה needs two listeners and another says three. It first suggests the argument depends on רבה בר רב הונא's rule that whatever is said before three people spreads anyway. It rejects that suggestion and gives two other explanations. Either they argue whether a מחאה made when the holder is absent counts, or they argue whether the listeners are formal עדות or are only there to make the matter known. Next comes the story of גידל בר מניומי. He protested before three rabbis, and when he came back a year later they told him one protest in the first year is enough. ריש לקיש, quoting בר קפרא, says the owner must protest again at the end of every three years. רבי יוחנן challenges this, asking how someone who is 'like a robber' could gain a חזקה. רבא rules like ריש לקיש. בר קפרא then teaches that repeated protests count only if they repeat the original claim. The amud ends as רבא, quoting רב נחמן, begins a rule that a מחאה is made before two people; his statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Suggestion that the two-or-three argument depends on רבה בר רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that the argument over two or three listeners depends on whether one accepts רבה בר רב הונא's rule about things said before three people.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...is not a problem of לשון הרע. So should we say: the one who says a מחאה needs two people does not agree with רבה בר רב הונא, and the one who says three people does agree with him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רבה בר רב הונא, who says that anything said in front of three people is not לשון הרע, because it will spread anyway. Then it suggests that this rule is the root of the argument over two versus three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The purpose of a מחאה is that word of it should reach the person holding the land. The opinion that requires three seems to rely on רבה בר רב הונא: news told to three people spreads, so it will reach the holder. The opinion that needs only two would then not hold of this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not hold of / he does hold of (someone's view)

phrases.english: is not subject to the problem of evil speech;
the one who says a protest is in front of two –

phrases.aramaic: לֵית לֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: does not hold of the view of Rabba bar Rav Huna,
and the one who says in front of three –

phrases.aramaic: אִית לֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא?
phrases.english: does hold of the view of Rabba bar Rav Huna?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר בִּפְנֵי שְׁנַיִם לֵית לֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a suggestion that started before this passage, linking the two-or-three argument to רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the argument over two or three listeners really about whether one accepts רבה בר רב הונא's rule?

steps.title: No — everyone agrees with רבה בר רב הונא; they argue about a מחאה made when the holder is not present
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone accepts רבה בר רב הונא. The real argument is whether a מחאה made when the holder is not there counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone holds of רבה בר רב הונא's view. Here they argue about this: the one who says two holds that a protest made not in the holder's presence is not a valid protest. The one who says three holds that a protest made not in his presence is a valid protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the first suggestion and gives a new reason for the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a מחאה only counts when the holder hears it directly, the listeners are only witnesses, so two are enough. If a מחאה counts even when the holder is absent, we need three people so the news is sure to spread back to him, using רבה בר רב הונא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A formal protest by the owner against someone holding his land
Not in his presence (the holder is not there)
He holds / he is of the opinion

phrases.english: No, everyone

phrases.aramaic: אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא;
phrases.english: holds of the view of Rabba bar Rav Huna;
and here, they argue about this –
the one who says in front of two holds:

phrases.aramaic: מֶחָאָה שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו לָא הָוְיָא מֶחָאָה.
phrases.english: a protest not in his presence is not a protest.
phrases.notes: "His" means the person living on the land, not the owner who is protesting.

phrases.english: And the one who says in front of three holds:
a protest not in his presence is a protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 1 and moves the argument to a different question.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that either side disagrees with רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The two-or-three argument can be explained even if everyone accepts רבה בר רב הונא. It depends on whether a מחאה made when the holder is absent is valid.

steps.title: Another explanation: formal testimony versus making the matter known
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, everyone agrees that a מחאה made when the holder is absent is valid. They argue whether we need עדות (two) or גילוי מילתא, making it publicly known (three).
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: everyone agrees that a protest not in his presence is a valid protest. Here they argue about this: the one who says two holds that we need testimony. The one who says three holds that we need the matter to be revealed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second, different way to explain the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both sides accept that the holder does not need to be present. The question is what the listeners are for. If they are formal witnesses, two are enough. If their job is to make the protest publicly known, three are needed so that it spreads.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (an alternative answer)
Revealing the matter / making it known

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain two versus three listeners for a מחאה: (1) whether a מחאה made when the holder is absent is valid; (2) whether the listeners serve as formal עדות or as a way to make the protest publicly known.

phrases.english: If you want, say: everyone agrees –
a protest not in his presence is a protest;
and here, they argue about this –
the one who says in front of two holds:
we need testimony.
And the one who says in front of three holds:
we need the matter to be revealed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second explanation, different from step 2, of the two-or-three argument.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument must depend on whether a מחאה made when the holder is absent is valid.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if both sides agree it is valid, they can argue about the listeners' role: formal witnesses or spreading the news.

steps.title: The story of גידל בר מניומי's protest
steps.stepSummary: גידל בר מניומי protested in front of three rabbis. A year later he came back to protest again.
steps.simpleTranslation: גידל בר מניומי had a protest to make. He found רב הונא, חייא בר רב and רב חלקיה בר טובי sitting together, and he protested in front of them. The next year he came back again to protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about a man making a מחאה. This sets up the question of whether he must protest again every year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He protested in front of three people, which satisfies even the opinion that requires three. The new issue is whether a מחאה has to be repeated each year, since חזקה is built over three years.

keyTerms.meaning: The next year / after a year

phrases.aramaic: גִּידֵּל בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי הֲוָה לֵיהּ מַחוּיָאתָה לְמַחוֹיֵי.
phrases.english: Giddel bar Minyumi had a protest to protest.

phrases.aramaic: אַשְׁכְּחִינְהוּ לְרַב הוּנָא וּלְחִיָּיא בַּר רַב
phrases.english: He found Rav Huna and Ḥiyya bar Rav

phrases.aramaic: וּלְרַב חִלְקִיָּה בַּר טוֹבִי דַּהֲווֹ יָתְבִי,
phrases.english: and Rav Ḥilkiya bar Tuvi, who were sitting,
and he protested before them.
A year later – he came again to protest,

steps.triggerLanguage: גִּידֵּל בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי הֲוָה לֵיהּ מַחוּיָאתָה לְמַחוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a story about a real מחאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: someone protested once in front of three rabbis and returned a year later to protest again.

steps.title: One protest in the first year is enough, in the name of רב
steps.stepSummary: The rabbis told him he did not need to protest again, because רב said one protest in the first year is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: You don't need to. This is what רב said: once he protested in the first year, he no longer needs to protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The rabbis answer גידל and quote רב: there is no need to repeat the מחאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single מחאה in the first year keeps protecting the owner. He does not have to protest again each year of the חזקה period.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a מחאה does not have to be repeated every year within the three-year period. Step 7 adds that the owner must still protest again at the end of each three-year period, and רבא rules that way in step 10.

phrases.english: They said to him: You don't need to,
this is what Rav said:
once he protested in the first year,
he no longer needs to protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ לָא צְרִיכַתְּ הָכִי אָמַר רַב
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One מחאה in the first year is enough; it does not need to be repeated (רב).

steps.title: Another version: חייא בר רב said the rule himself
steps.stepSummary: Some say it was חייא בר רב who told him this, on his own, not quoting רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: חייא בר רב said to him: once he protested in the first year, he no longer needs to protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of who gave the answer. The ruling itself stays the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the source of the ruling changes. In the first version all three rabbis quote רב. In this version חייא בר רב says it himself.
steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree on the rule: a מחאה made in the first year does not need to be repeated. They differ only on who said it.

phrases.english: And there are those who say,
Ḥiyya bar Rav said to him:
once he protested in the first year,
he no longer needs to protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ חִיָּיא בַּר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of who said the ruling in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חייא בר רב himself rules that a מחאה in the first year is enough.

steps.title: The owner must protest again every three years
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש, quoting בר קפרא, says one protest is not enough forever. The owner must protest again at the end of every three-year period.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said in the name of בר קפרא: The owner must protest at the end of every three years.
steps.whatsHappening: A new opinion is brought. One protest does not protect the owner forever, so he has to protect his claim again every three years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said one protest in the first year is enough. ריש לקיש adds a time limit: that protest only covers three years. If the owner stays silent for a new full three years, the holder can again gain a חזקה.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא from ארץ ישראל, the study partner of רבי יוחנן
A sage from the time right after the משנה was finished
To protest, to openly declare that the land is still yours

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the owner must protest every day or every year. He only needs to make sure the holder never has three full years in a row with no protest.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם בַּר קַפָּרָא:
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said in the name of Bar Kappara:
And he needs to protest
at the end of each and every three [years].
phrases.notes: 'Years' is not written, but it is understood: each three-year stretch of the holder living there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם בַּר קַפָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit to רב's rule that one protest is enough.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A protest protects the owner for only three years. He must protest again at the end of each three-year period.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן is surprised: can a robber gain ownership?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן finds ריש לקיש's rule strange. Once the owner protested, the holder is like a thief. How could a thief ever gain a חזקה?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן wondered about it: Does a robber have a חזקה?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן attacks ריש לקיש's rule. He argues that one protest should be enough forever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The protest shows that the holder is on the land against the owner's will. Someone like that should never be able to build a חזקה, no matter how many years pass. So why would the owner need to protest again?

keyTerms.meaning: The leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל
A robber, one who takes property by force

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan wondered at it:
But does a robber have a chazaka?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges ריש לקיש's rule from step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's rule that the owner must protest every three years
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once the owner protested, the holder is like a robber. A robber can never gain a חזקה, so a second protest should not be needed.

steps.title: Fixing the wording: not a robber, but like a robber
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the holder is not truly a גזלן, since nothing was proven. רבי יוחנן's question really means: can someone who only looks like a robber gain a חזקה?
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you think he is really a robber?! Rather, the question is: Does someone who is like a robber have a חזקה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא corrects the wording of רבי יוחנן's question so that it makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A protest does not prove that the holder stole anything. It only makes him look suspicious. So רבי יוחנן's point is that once the holder is in this 'like a robber' position, he still should not be able to gain a חזקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? A way of rejecting an idea
Like a robber, someone who only looks like a thief

phrases.english: "A robber" — could that enter your mind?!
Rather: does one who is "like a robber" have a chazaka?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Corrects the wording of the challenge in step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן was calling the holder a real robber.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant the holder only looks like a robber because of the protest.

steps.title: רבא rules: protest every three years
steps.stepSummary: רבא decides the הלכה follows ריש לקיש and בר קפרא. The owner must protest at the end of every three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is that he must protest at the end of every three years.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the final ruling in the argument between ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though רבי יוחנן was surprised, the הלכה follows ריש לקיש. An old protest does not protect the owner forever. He must renew it before each new three-year period ends.

keyTerms.meaning: A major אמורא of בבל whose rulings are often the final הלכה

steps.whatToRemember: The final הלכה: an owner must protest at the end of each three-year period, or the holder can gain a חזקה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: an owner cannot rely on one old protest forever.

phrases.english: Rava said: The halacha is —

phrases.aramaic: צָרִיךְ לְמַחוֹת בְּסוֹף כׇּל שָׁלֹשׁ וְשָׁלֹשׁ.
phrases.english: he needs to protest at the end of each and every three [years].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument in favor of ריש לקיש, against רבי יוחנן's surprise.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows ריש לקיש: the owner must protest again at the end of every three years.

steps.title: Repeated protests must repeat the same claim
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא teaches that if the owner protested several times, it depends on what he said. If every protest repeated his first claim, the holder has no חזקה. If he switched to new claims, the holder does have a חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא taught: If he protested, and protested again, and protested again, then: if he protested because of the first claim, the holder has no חזקה. If not, the holder has a חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching from בר קפרא explains when repeated protests work. They must all stick to the same claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Protesting again is only useful if the owner keeps saying the same thing. If he keeps changing his story, each new claim cancels the earlier ones. Then the protests do not count, and the holder keeps his חזקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught, introducing a teaching from the time of the תנאים
He challenged or protested the holder's right
The first claim, the original reason the owner gave

steps.confusionAlert: 'He has' / 'he has no' חזקה is about the holder, not about the owner who protested.

phrases.english: Bar Kappara taught:
If he protested, then protested again, then protested again —
if he protested based on the first claim,
he has no chazaka.
phrases.notes: 'He' here is the person living on the land. The owner's protests stopped him from gaining ownership.

phrases.english: And if not, he has a chazaka.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a condition to the rule of repeated protests from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Repeated protests prevent a חזקה only if they repeat the original claim. New, different claims cancel the earlier ones, and the holder gains a חזקה.

steps.title: A protest is made in front of two people
steps.stepSummary: רבא, quoting רב נחמן, begins a rule about how a מחאה is done: it is made in front of two people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: A protest is made in front of two people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new rule about how many people must hear a protest. This line sets up a statement that continues in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects back to steps 1–3, which explained the argument over whether a מחאה needs two listeners or three. רב נחמן starts by saying two are enough. The rest of his statement comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading אמורא of בבל, expert in monetary law
A protest declaring that the land still belongs to you

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Nachman said:
A protest — in front of two,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how often to protest to how many people must be present.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מחאה can be made in front of two people. The statement continues in the next lines.
